paragraphs: This checklist is for self-questioning only and does not constitute hiring criteria, ability scores, or safety evaluation conclusions. This page is written according to the U.S. O*NET-SOC 33-1011.00 “First-Line Supervisors of Correctional Officers” (the fixed index assigns this asset the Chinese occupational name for this occupation, and the body text follows that official occupational scope). Even within correctional facility supervision, the differences are large: prisons and jails, detention and pretrial facilities, juvenile correction and rehabilitation institutions, community corrections and probation supervision, escort and transport assignments, and correctional technology and record management positions; a supervisor may lead only one shift or simultaneously manage several housing units and posts. Before comparing positions or development paths, first check: the education and enforcement training required for the role, whether enforcement or correctional position qualifications and pre-service training are required, physical fitness test and background check standards, the duty and shift system (including night shifts and holidays), and the authorization and procedural requirements for using force and weapons.

Validate with one paper exercise: you are given a completely fictitious correctional assignment (facility type and inmate population size, the number of personnel on shift and post assignments, the roll calls and counts to be carried out, an inmate conflict or contraband discovery incident, available monitoring and communication means, and the records and reporting required). You are asked to write out the shift deployment and post arrangements, order and safety key points, the incident handling and escalation sequence, the records and reports to be used, and how to coordinate with higher headquarters and other posts, and to mark which decisions must be made by higher levels or personnel holding statutory authority.

Signals worth considering more: able to work long term in a closed correctional environment, able to stay calm under conflict and pressure and hold to procedures, and willing to manage others according to rules and discipline and to record truthfully. Signals requiring caution: unwillingness to face an adversarial population over the long term, difficulty controlling emotions under high pressure, and imagining correctional work as only watching monitors in an office.
This card is a career exploration reference and does not constitute hiring, ability scoring, safety, or enforcement conclusions.

First judge whether you are willing to make order and safety management in a correctional facility a long-term career: it requires facing an adversarial population over the long term, maintaining discipline according to rules and procedures, organizing shifts and post assignments, and bearing supervisory responsibility for the safety of inmates and colleagues; validate with the paper exercise and seven-day task on this page.

The work of first-line supervisors of correctional officers revolves around the cycle of “handover and roll call—deployment and assignment—supervision and patrol—incident handling and escalation—records and evaluation”: on arriving for duty, complete the handover and the count of equipment and keys, organize the roll call and headcount and verify the number of inmates; assign shift duties by housing unit and post and specify order, safety, and discipline requirements; patrol housing units, workshops, and common areas, supervise inmate behavior and subordinates' duty status, and carry out searches and contraband seizures; for incidents such as conflicts, violence, escapes, and self-harm, take initial action according to procedure and escalate within authorization, using force lawfully when necessary; review inmate information to identify those requiring focused attention and arrange corresponding controls; complete shift records, incident reports, and reports, and train and mentor subordinates and evaluate their performance. The emphasis differs greatly by direction: the prison and jail direction stresses roll call and order management, the escort and transport direction stresses route safety and handover, the juvenile correction direction stresses behavior guidance and coordination with education, the community corrections direction stresses supervision and reporting, and the correctional technology direction stresses monitoring systems and record management.
U.S. O*NET-SOC 33-1011.00 “First-Line Supervisors of Correctional Officers”: directly supervise and coordinate the work of correctional officers and jailers.

Work context | First-line supervisors of correctional officers focus on on-site supervision in correctional facilities and must manage order, people, and records at the same time. O*NET work context shows that work schedules are mostly regular (87% regular), with 13% irregular; among weekly work hours, 47% exceed 40 hours and 53% are 40 hours; 84% maintain continuous contact with others; 86% have face-to-face discussions every day; 92% have telephone conversations every day; 69% consider the work to require extremely precise or highly accurate work combined (37% extremely important, 32% very important); the consequences of error are extremely serious for 30%, very serious for 22%, and serious for 18%; 42% have strict deadlines every day; conflict situations occur every day for 66%; 70% must deal with unpleasant, angry, or discourteous people every day; 57% must deal with people with violent or physically aggressive tendencies every day; 77% have very high responsibility for the health and safety of others and 23% high responsibility; 74% must make decisions every day; the degree of automation of the work is 49% not at all automated, 19% slightly, and 26% moderately; 86% work indoors in a controlled environment every day; 37% work outdoors in all weather every day; 53% are exposed to noise every day; 53% are exposed to disease or infection every day; 33% are exposed to contaminants every day.

Main objects | Inmates and detainees, subordinate correctional officers and same-shift colleagues, housing units, workshops, and common areas, monitoring and communication equipment, keys and access control, contraband and case-related items, and records and reports.

Collaboration | Collaboration with higher-level supervisors and duty officers, same-shift and relieving correctional officers, medical and psychological service personnel, education, social work, and treatment personnel, case-handling and judicial personnel, and visiting family members.

Tools and materials | Housing unit access control and keys, monitoring and alarm systems, communications and intercom equipment, restraint and protective equipment, search implements and detection devices, and record forms and correctional information systems.

Institutional basis | Correctional facility management and safety rules, inmate management and discipline regulations, authorization and procedures for the use of force and weapons, occupational health and safety requirements, and record and information confidentiality rules.

Record requirements | Shift handover records, roll call and count records, patrol and search records, incident and handling records, use of force records, and training and assessment records must be kept on file according to institutional rules.

Practice boundaries | Restricting personal liberty, using force and weapons, and decisions on handling inmates must be made under law and authorized procedures and carried out by personnel and agencies with statutory authority; this page does not provide operational advice on enforcement, safety, or handling tactics.

Environment and pace | Correctional facilities are closed and highly adversarial and involve risks such as violent assault, disease and infection, and psychological pressure; duty often uses a shift system including night shifts and holidays, and incident handling times are concentrated and unpredictable.

Region and scope | U.S. O*NET-SOC 33-1011.00 does not map one-to-one onto mainland China's occupational classification; the establishment, enforcement qualifications, training, and assessment requirements of the mainland's prison and judicial administrative people's police must be verified separately according to local and competent department regulations.

entries.answer: This page is written according to the U.S. O*NET-SOC 33-1011.00 “First-Line Supervisors of Correctional Officers” (the fixed index assigns this asset the Chinese occupational name for this occupation): directly supervise and coordinate the work of correctional officers and jailers. Specifically this includes: on arriving for duty, completing the handover and the count of equipment and keys, organizing the roll call and headcount and verifying the number of inmates; assigning shift duties by housing unit and post and specifying order, safety, and discipline requirements; patrolling housing units, workshops, and common areas, supervising inmate behavior and subordinates' duty status, and organizing or taking part in searches and contraband seizures; taking initial action on incidents such as conflicts, violence, escapes, and self-harm according to procedure and escalating within authorization, using force lawfully when necessary; reviewing inmate information to identify those requiring focused attention; completing shift records, incident reports, and reports; and training and mentoring subordinates and evaluating their duty performance.
entries.question: What do First-Line Supervisors of Correctional Officers mainly do?

entries.answer: Primary tasks and authority differ: this occupation's main output is the order and safety supervision of inmates within correctional facilities and the management of subordinates' duty, and it is a first-line management position; correctional officers and jailers produce the daily duty of directly guarding and supervising inmates; first-line supervisors of police and detectives and police and sheriff's patrol officers produce public order, patrol, and criminal enforcement; probation officers and correctional treatment specialists focus on community corrections supervision and treatment services; bailiffs focus on courtroom security and transport; emergency management directors focus on plan development and interagency coordination; and first-line supervisors of security workers focus on managing protective services at commercial venues.
entries.question: How does it differ from correctional officers and jailers and first-line supervisors of police and detectives?

entries.answer: U.S. O*NET-SOC 33-1011.00 “First-Line Supervisors of Correctional Officers”: interest code ECS, Job Zone 3 (medium preparation, SVP 6.0 to <7.0), not marked Bright Outlook (projected decline for 2024—2034). Work context shows that work schedules are mostly regular (87% regular), with 13% irregular; among weekly work hours, 47% exceed 40 hours and 53% are 40 hours; 84% maintain continuous contact with others; 86% have face-to-face discussions every day; 92% have telephone conversations every day; 69% consider the work to require extremely precise or highly accurate work combined; the consequences of error are extremely serious for 30%, very serious for 22%, and serious for 18%; 42% have strict deadlines every day; conflict situations occur every day for 66%; 70% must deal with unpleasant, angry, or discourteous people every day; 57% must deal with people with violent or physically aggressive tendencies every day; 77% have very high responsibility for the health and safety of others and 23% high responsibility; 74% must make decisions every day; the degree of automation of the work is 49% not at all automated, 19% slightly, and 26% moderately; 86% work indoors in a controlled environment every day; 37% work outdoors in all weather every day; 53% are exposed to noise every day; 53% are exposed to disease or infection every day; 33% are exposed to contaminants every day.

entries.answer: The more accurate judgment is that steps such as scheduling and roll call statistics, monitoring data aggregation, record and report organization, and training material drafting will be taken over by tools, and the occupation as a whole will mainly see augmentation. The ILO 2023 study shows that task exposure varies greatly across occupations, that the share of highly exposed tasks in managerial and professional occupations is relatively low, and that technical feasibility does not mean agencies have already adopted it; order judgment, use of force authorization, on-site safety, and responsibility must be borne by trained personnel with statutory authority, so the conclusion is that the way of working will change, not that the occupation as a whole will be replaced.

entries.answer: Responsibility for on-shift on-site safety and order management is borne by the watch supervisor; restricting personal liberty, using force and weapons, and decisions on handling inmates must be made under law and authorized procedures and carried out by personnel and agencies with statutory authority. Information and monitoring images must be handled according to minimum necessity and confidentiality rules. When using monitoring and information systems, tool outputs do not constitute enforcement decisions or incident characterization, and matters beyond one's authorized scope should be reported to higher headquarters. subject.name: First-Line Supervisors of Correctional Officers
subject.summary: Directly supervise and coordinate the work of correctional officers and jailers: includes organizing roll calls and counts as required, maintaining order and discipline in housing units, arranging shifts and post assignments, supervising and taking part in searches and contraband seizures, organizing response and handling in emergencies such as escapes and violence, reviewing inmate information and identifying those requiring focused attention, supervising the completion and retention of records and reports, and training and mentoring subordinates and evaluating their performance.
